lead: Solution thermodynamics answers one question: how does a component's escaping tendency change with composition? You will build the chain chemical potential → partial molar properties → fugacity → activity, and use it to calculate phase equilibrium for real mixtures. After this unit you can compute partial molar volumes, fugacity coefficients, activities, excess properties and simple vapour-liquid equilibrium compositions.
about: This unit turns Gibbs free energy into a tool for mixtures. Chapter 5.1 defines chemical potential and the equality that fixes phase equilibrium. Chapter 5.2 introduces partial molar properties, and 5.3 shows they cannot vary independently through the Gibbs-Duhem equation. Chapter 5.4 replaces pressure by fugacity, so real gases can be handled. Chapter 5.5 applies the Lewis-Randall rule to ideal solutions and marks where real solutions deviate. Chapter 5.6 measures those deviations with excess properties and property changes of mixing. Chapter 5.7 converts them into activity and activity coefficients, the working variables for VLE. Chapter 5.8, taught in only a few universities, fits Margules, van Laar and Wilson models to activity coefficient data. After the unit you can calculate μ, partial molar volumes, fugacities, activities and simple VLE compositions.

chapters.idea: Chemical potential μ is the partial molar Gibbs energy, and at equilibrium a species has the same μ in every phase.
chapters.depth: Define μ_i = (∂G/∂n_i)_{T,P,n_j} for species i. Derive dG = −S dT + V dP + Σ μ_i dn_i. Obtain phase-equilibrium criterion μ_i^α = μ_i^β and the direction of spontaneous transfer from higher to lower μ. Cover pure components and mixtures. Some syllabi call μ the partial molar Gibbs energy or escaping tendency. Keep stability proof short.

figure.title: Chemical potential decides transfer
figure.aria: A block diagram with liquid A at 100.0 kJ/mol and vapour A at 101.5 kJ/mol, showing net transfer from vapour to liquid until the chemical potentials become equal.

chapters.example: At 300 K, μ_A(liquid) = 100.0 kJ/mol and μ_A(vapour) = 101.5 kJ/mol. Find ΔG when 0.010 mol of A moves from vapour to liquid. The transfer gives ΔG = (100.0 − 101.5) × 0.010 = −0.015 kJ = −15 J, so vapour moves to liquid spontaneously.
chapters.trap: Using μ only for pure substances; in a mixture μ depends on composition. A higher μ means higher escaping tendency, not higher concentration.
chapters.prereq: Unit 4: Gibbs free energy and fundamental property relations; Unit 1: intensive and extensive variables.
chapters.leave: Fugacity calculations to Chapter 5.4; phase rule and Duhem's theorem to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A partial molar property is the contribution of one mole of a component to a mixture property at fixed T, P and other moles.
chapters.depth: Define M̄_i = (∂(nM)/∂n_i)_{T,P,n_j}. Show total M = Σ x_i M̄_i. Teach the tangent-intercept construction on an M versus x₁ plot. Cover partial molar volume, enthalpy, entropy and Gibbs energy; note μ_i = Ḡ_i. Use binary formulas M̄₁ = M + x₂ dM/dx₁ and M̄₂ = M − x₁ dM/dx₁.

figure.aria: A plot of molar volume against x₁ for V = 18 + 28x₁ − 6x₁², with the tangent at x₁=0.25 whose intercepts give partial molar volumes 43.375 and 18.375 cm³/mol.

chapters.example: For a binary mixture at 298 K, V = 40x₁ + 18x₂ + 6x₁x₂ cm³/mol. Find the partial molar volumes at x₁ = 0.25. Here x₂ = 0.75, V = 24.625 cm³/mol and dV/dx₁ = 28 − 12x₁ = 25.0. Then V̄₁ = 24.625 + 0.75 × 25 = 43.375 cm³/mol and V̄₂ = 24.625 − 0.25 × 25 = 18.375 cm³/mol.
chapters.trap: Forgetting that partial molar properties change with composition; do not use pure-component values in mixture sums.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.1; Unit 4: partial derivatives and Gibbs free energy.
chapters.leave: Density measurements and VLE data reduction to later chapters and Unit 6.

chapters.idea: At fixed T and P, the partial molar properties in a mixture are not independent; they obey Σ x_i dM̄_i = 0.
chapters.depth: Derive the Gibbs-Duhem equation from homogeneity and Euler's theorem, then differentiate at fixed T and P. For Gibbs energy write Σ x_i dμ_i = 0. Give binary form x₁dM̄₁ + x₂dM̄₂ = 0. Show use for checking slopes and consistency of VLE data. Some syllabi call it the Duhem relation.

figure.title: From homogeneity to Gibbs-Duhem
figure.aria: A vertical flow from a homogeneous property through Euler's theorem and differentiation to the Gibbs-Duhem equation, ending with the example slopes −30 and +20.

chapters.example: At fixed T and P, a binary mixture has x₁ = 0.40, x₂ = 0.60 and dM̄₁/dx₁ = −30.0 kJ mol⁻¹ per unit x₁. Find dM̄₂/dx₁. Gibbs-Duhem gives x₁dM̄₁ + x₂dM̄₂ = 0, so dM̄₂/dx₁ = −(0.40/0.60)(−30.0) = +20.0 kJ mol⁻¹ per unit x₁.
chapters.trap: Dropping constant T and P; Gibbs-Duhem is not Σ x_i M̄_i = 0, it is Σ x_i dM̄_i = 0.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.2; homogeneous functions and Euler's theorem from mathematics.
chapters.leave: Full thermodynamic consistency tests of VLE data sets to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Fugacity f is the corrected pressure that keeps the chemical potential formula valid for real gases.
chapters.depth: Define f_i by μ_i = μ_i° + RT ln(f_i/f_i°), with f_i → P_i as P → 0. Define φ_i = f_i/P_i. Derive ln φ = (1/RT)∫(V − RT/P)dP = ∫(Z − 1)dP/P. Cover pure and mixture fugacity, residual Gibbs energy relation, and a brief generalized correlation. Some syllabi call φ the fugacity coefficient.

figure.aria: A plot of fugacity coefficient against pressure from 1 to 10 bar for constant Z = 0.90, falling from 1.000 to 0.794.

chapters.example: A pure gas at 10.0 bar has Z = 0.90 constant from 1 to 10 bar. Taking the ideal-gas reference at 1 bar, estimate φ and f at 10.0 bar. ln φ = (0.90 − 1)ln(10/1) = −0.230, so φ = 0.794 and f = φP = 0.794 × 10.0 = 7.94 bar.
chapters.trap: Setting f = P for real gases; φ = 1 only in the ideal-gas limit. Use one reference state consistently.
chapters.prereq: Unit 4: residual properties; Unit 2: compressibility factor and equations of state; Chapter 5.1 for μ.
chapters.leave: Cubic EOS derivations to Unit 2; high-pressure VLE algorithms to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: An ideal solution follows the Lewis-Randall rule f_i = x_i f_i^pure, and real solutions deviate from it.
chapters.depth: Define ideal solution by μ_i = μ_i^pure + RT ln x_i. State the Lewis-Randall rule f_i = x_i f_i^pure and Raoult's law at low pressure. Compare ideal-gas mixtures with ideal solutions. Cover positive and negative deviations from Raoult's law and Henry's law as the dilute limit. Mention standard states.

figure.aria: A pressure-composition diagram with bubble pressure 40 + 60x₁ and dew pressure 1/(y₁/100 + (1−y₁)/40), meeting at 58 kPa for x₁=0.30 and y₁=0.517.

chapters.example: At 350 K, pure component 1 has P₁sat = 100 kPa and component 2 has P₂sat = 40 kPa. An ideal liquid has x₁ = 0.30. Find p₁, p₂, total P and vapour y₁. p₁ = 0.30 × 100 = 30 kPa, p₂ = 0.70 × 40 = 28 kPa, P = 58 kPa, and y₁ = 30/58 = 0.517.
chapters.trap: Confusing an ideal solution with an ideal gas; an ideal solution has zero heat and volume change of mixing, not zero intermolecular forces.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.4; Unit 2 ideal gas; Unit 6 Raoult and Henry laws used as reference.
chapters.leave: Azeotrope and full bubble/dew calculations to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Excess properties measure how far a real mixture is from an ideal solution at the same T, P and composition.
chapters.depth: Define ΔM_mix = M − Σ x_i M_i^pure and M^E = ΔM_mix − ΔM_mix,ideal. Cover G^E = RTΣ x_i ln γ_i, H^E, V^E and S^E. Treat heats of mixing and volume changes of mixing. Show use of excess Gibbs energy to obtain activity coefficients later.

figure.aria: A plot of excess volume V^E = 2x₁x₂ against x₁, with a maximum of 0.500 cm³/mol at x₁ = 0.50.

chapters.example: For a binary liquid, V^E = 2x₁x₂ cm³/mol. At x₁ = 0.50, find ΔV_mix for 2.00 mol of mixture. V^E = 2 × 0.50 × 0.50 = 0.500 cm³/mol. For an ideal solution ΔV_mix,ideal = 0, so ΔV_mix = 0.500 cm³/mol. For 2.00 mol, total ΔV = 1.00 cm³.
chapters.trap: Adding excess and ideal mixing changes with the wrong sign or per-mole basis; check whether the value is per mole of mixture or total moles.
chapters.leave: Calorimetric measurement and plant enthalpy balances to Unit 1 and Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Activity a_i replaces mole fraction in the chemical potential, and γ_i = a_i/x_i measures non-ideality.
chapters.depth: Define a_i = f_i/f_i° and γ_i = a_i/x_i. Write μ_i = μ_i° + RT ln a_i = μ_i° + RT ln(γ_i x_i). Cover pure-liquid and Henry standard states. Obtain γ_i from VLE using y_iP = γ_i x_i P_i^sat at low pressure. Relate ln γ_i to excess Gibbs energy.

figure.title: From fugacity to activity coefficient
figure.aria: A block diagram converting f₁ = 0.50 bar and f₁° = 0.80 bar into activity a₁ = 0.625 and then activity coefficient γ₁ = 3.125 at x₁ = 0.20.

chapters.example: At 1.00 bar total pressure, a binary VLE has x₁ = 0.20, y₁ = 0.50 and P₁sat = 0.80 bar. The vapour is ideal and the liquid standard state is pure component at its saturation pressure. Find a₁ and γ₁. f₁ = y₁P = 0.50 bar, f₁° = P₁sat = 0.80 bar, so a₁ = 0.50/0.80 = 0.625 and γ₁ = 0.625/0.20 = 3.125.
chapters.trap: Using a_i = x_i for non-ideal solutions; γ_i = 1 only for an ideal solution, and the chosen standard state changes γ_i.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 5.4 and 5.6; Unit 6 VLE relation yP = γxPsat.
chapters.leave: Ionic activity coefficients and Debye-Hückel theory to electrochemistry; full VLE algorithms to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Margules, van Laar and Wilson equations are activity coefficient models built from excess Gibbs energy.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this; keep it short. Give two-suffix Margules G^E/RT = A x₁x₂, ln γ₁ = A x₂², ln γ₂ = A x₁². Give van Laar with constants A₁₂ and A₂₁. Give Wilson local-composition form with Λ₁₂ and Λ₂₁. Show fitting one or two parameters to γ data and use for non-ideal VLE. Mention limits of each model.

figure.aria: Two curves for the two-suffix Margules model with A = 0.80, giving γ₁ = 1.480 and γ₂ = 1.075 at x₁ = 0.30.

chapters.example: For a binary mixture fitted by the two-suffix Margules equation with A = 0.80, find γ₁ and γ₂ at x₁ = 0.30. ln γ₁ = A x₂² = 0.80 × 0.70² = 0.392, so γ₁ = 1.480. ln γ₂ = A x₁² = 0.80 × 0.30² = 0.072, so γ₂ = 1.075.
chapters.trap: Using fitted constants outside the measured composition or temperature range; Margules and van Laar constants are not universal, and Wilson has model-specific limits.
chapters.leave: UNIQUAC, UNIFAC and parameter regression to advanced courses.
